3.1.1.locator: GDPR resource center, encryption-in-transit passage: '...applied by default on Google Cloud to encrypt requests before transmission and to protect the raw data using the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol'
3.1.1.notes: Real standard: TLS (HTTPS), applied by default. The Cloud DPA Appendix 2 'Encryption Technologies' also states 'Google makes HTTPS encryption (also referred to as SSL or TLS connection) available. Google servers support ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman cryptographic key exchange signed with RSA and ECDSA' (perfect forward secrecy). Neither fetched source states a TLS protocol VERSION, so per the hard rules the versioned dropdown options (TLS 1.2 / TLS 1.3) cannot be selected. Google's 'Encryption in transit' whitepaper, which documents versions, lives at https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/security/encryption-in-transit and was unreachable this session (host blocked by the network proxy, HTTP 403 on CONNECT). A human with normal network access should confirm the version from that whitepaper before submission.

3.1.2.notes: Encryption at rest by default IS documented: 'Once data is transferred to Google Cloud to be stored, Google Cloud applies encryption at rest by default' and 'Google Workspace and Google Cloud services encrypt customer content stored at rest, without any action required from customers, using one or more encryption mechanisms' (https://cloud.google.com/privacy/gdpr, fetched this session). However, no page fetchable this session states the algorithm/standard. Google's 'Default encryption at rest' whitepaper (https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/security/encryption/default-encryption and the PDF under .../resources/encryption-whitepaper.pdf) documents the algorithm but the docs.cloud.google.com host was blocked by the session's network proxy (403 on CONNECT), so per the hard rules the standard cannot be asserted here. Searched: cloud.google.com/privacy/gdpr, cloud.google.com/terms/data-processing-addendum (the only AES statement, 'at least AES128 or similar', is specific to the Google Distributed Cloud connected product amendment, not general GCP), cloud.google.com/trust-center, cloud.google.com/trust-center/security, cloud.google.com/security. A human should pull the standard from the default-encryption whitepaper and upgrade this cell.

3.1.3.notes: Backup encryption is not documented separately from general encryption at rest on any primary source fetched this session. Searched: https://cloud.google.com/terms/data-processing-addendum (Appendix 2; 'backup' hits concern backup power/generators only), https://cloud.google.com/privacy/gdpr, https://cloud.google.com/trust-center/security. Per the field playbook, 'Not known' is the common and correct answer here. Ask the vendor in writing or confirm from the default-encryption whitepaper whether backups are covered by the same at-rest encryption.

3.1.4.locator: GDPR resource center, Encryption section: default encryption at rest 'without any action required from customers' (i.e. Google-managed default keys)
3.1.4.notes: Google's default encryption at rest requires no customer action, i.e. Google generates and manages the keys. Customer-controlled options exist and are documented on Google's Cloud Key Management product page (https://cloud.google.com/security/products/security-key-management, fetched this session): customer-managed keys via Cloud KMS (CMEK), FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated Cloud HSM, and external keys via Cloud EKM. Per the playbook, the answer flips to 'Key generated by your company' only if Tavus actually uses CMEK/BYOK for the workloads in scope - CHECK WITH THE HUMAN before filling the workbook.

3.1.6.locator: Sensitive Data Protection product page: 'De-identification, masking, tokenization, and bucketing... De-identification enables you to transform your data to reduce data risk'; re-identification risk analysis including 'Computing k-anonymity for a dataset'
3.1.6.notes: Capability exists as a customer-configurable Google Cloud service (Sensitive Data Protection / Cloud DLP): de-identification, redaction, masking, and k-anonymity/l-diversity risk analysis. It is not applied automatically - Tavus would have to configure it. Google does not anonymize customer data on Tavus's behalf as part of basic infrastructure hosting.

3.1.7.locator: Sensitive Data Protection product page: 'De-identification techniques like tokenization (pseudonymization) let you preserve the utility of your data for joining or analytics, while reducing the risk of handling the data, by obfuscating the raw sensitive identifiers.'
3.1.7.notes: Pseudonymization named explicitly (tokenization) on Google's own product page fetched this session. Same caveat as 3.1.6: a customer-configurable service, not a default behavior of the hosting.
